In educational settings, traditional lectures incorporating live demonstrations offer an effective way to convey information. However, the natural language descriptions used to present these demonstrations can sometimes confuse the audience, leading to misinterpretations. To address this issue, our research has created a novel dataset called Multimodal Lecture Demonstrations (MLD), which includes synchronized video, audio, and slide captures to facilitate hands-on learning. The dataset comprises 100 lectures from diverse fields and features various demonstration techniques, making it a valuable resource for machine learning. To facilitate further development, our work has explored the application of image processing and neural networks to analyze and understand these lectures. Specifically, our studies have investigated the role of visual cues in educational settings, while also examining the potential of neural networks to decode multimodal information from the MLD dataset. Our research has shown that combining visual cues with neural networks can significantly enhance the accuracy of these analyses. The ultimate goal of this work is to provide a foundation for the creation of advanced educational tools leveraging multimodal information. The University of Connecticut's Center for the Education of Teachers (CET) has developed the "Center-based Evaluation of Teacher Education Program" (CTEP) project, which aims to enhance teacher education through the use of innovative assessment methods, including the Benoit-Diaz and the National Council of Academic Practitioners (NCPED) multi-stem free response questions. To support this initiative, the CET has created "ServiceX," an assessment data transformation system that enables the analysis of large datasets from free response questions. In this presentation, we will discuss the advancements made towards automating free response question analysis and demonstrate ServiceX's capabilities by applying it to free response questions from the 2020 National Survey of Teacher and Pre-service Teacher. The findings reveal significant disparities in teacher diversity and representation, as well as a lack of diversity in the content of student writing. Our research data and ServiceX software are available for public use, with the software itself being open-source and freely downloadable. ServiceX is available for download at https://github.com/ucfced/servicesX. Our research team is also happy to provide hands-on experience with ServiceX at ASHE meeting room 10510, and the software's source code can be accessed at our public GitHub repository. ServiceX is licensed under the MIT open-source software license for public use. For more information, please contact our lead author, Dr. Maria Hernandez-Guerrero, at [Maria.Hernandez-Guerrero@uconn.edu]. Botnets, consisting of numerous compromised computers, pose a significant threat, making it challenging to identify them through traditional methods. The presence of botnets enables malicious actors to spread spam, steal data, and even hack into critical infrastructure. The unique nature of botnet activity, derived from their automated commands, offers a means to detect their presence. This paper explores the utilization of natural language processing techniques for botnet detection, utilizing command logs from honeypots to identify suspicious activity. Furthermore, the research employs a semantic analysis to categorize commands, enabling the detection of coordinated bot activities. The developed system successfully detected several botnets operating on the Tor network in real-time. The source code for this research is available on GitHub. This thesis delves into the visual object recognition within the realm of document image analysis. It begins with a comprehensive review of existing techniques for identifying shapes, text, and symbols across three distinct domains - computer vision, pattern recognition, and document image analysis - highlighting their respective applications and limitations. Building upon this analysis, the identification of shapes in document images is explored in depth, encompassing the categorization of geometric shapes, the recognition of known shapes, and the recognition of unknown shapes. Conversely, the recognition of text and symbols is approached from two perspectives: the segmentation of text and symbols, followed by the classification of text and symbols. Novel contributions are made in each area, accompanied by experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed approaches. Furthermore, the thesis extends its scope to encompass the identification of visual objects within the context of document image understanding, outlining the relevance of object recognition to this broader field. Ultimately, the thesis concludes by reflecting on the key findings and highlighting potential areas for future investigation in this field. This paper presents the design and implementation of VGStore and showcases its performance on a comprehensive multimedia analysis dataset. The study of superposition calculi for automated theorem proving has seen significant advancements. A key factor in the success of these calculi is their ability to generate large and efficient proof transitions through the effective use of rule combinations. This paper examines a set of calculi known as AC$^*$, which incorporate specific rule combinations to facilitate efficient proof generation for equational theories. By utilizing a novel approach to managing term rewrites within the reduction step, these calculi are able to produce a broader range of proof transitions while maintaining soundness. A critical aspect of the calculi is the application of closure overlap, which involves combining multiple proof fragments to facilitate the derivation of effective proof transitions. An examination of the calculi reveals that AC$^*$-reduction, a core component of the calculi, is a semantical equivalent of the full EAC$^*$ calculus. Furthermore, this study provides insights into the generation of proof transitions through the application of closure overlap, highlighting its role in the derivation of effective AC$^*$ calculi. Empirical evaluations of the calculi on a set of real-world examples demonstrate their ability to produce concise and efficient proof transitions. By integrating the study with existing research on EAC$^*$ and rewriting, these results provide valuable contributions to the field. Finally, this study presents a generalized framework for AC$^*$ reduction, which can be applied to derive various effective calculi for automated theorem proving. Investigating brain connectivity using resting-state fMRI is a rapidly evolving field, with numerous studies employing various analysis approaches.  A primary analysis technique involves aggregating data from multiple brain regions to form networks for further study.  A significant challenge in this process is determining the optimal number of brain sites to include, due to considerations of both data reliability and analysis power.  In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, termed statistical strength, which quantifies the reliability of connectivity estimates based on the number of brain sites analyzed.  We demonstrate that this metric is closely linked to the accuracy of network structure predictions and provide an efficient method for computing network predictions that align with observed data.  Notably, our proposed metric diverges from other network measures, such as network efficiency, which also assess network structure predictions.  We further demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional methods in both data reliability and analysis power when applied to resting-state fMRI data collected from 1,216 individuals.  Specifically, our results show that incorporating more brain regions of interest yields more accurate network structure predictions.  Conversely, our proposed approach yields more accurate network structure predictions with fewer brain regions than traditional methods.  These findings underscore the importance of considering the optimal number of brain regions for achieving reliable and powerful network connectivity findings in resting-state fMRI data. This method capitalizes on the underlying knowledge shared among various bird species tasks, utilizing a single neural network to streamline training and runtime efficiency. A cache vulnerability allows an attacker to infer confidential data by exploiting the timing of software execution, which can cause security issues and raise concerns about maintaining confidentiality. In this study, we introduce CacheQL, a system that comprehensively evaluates cache side-channel vulnerabilities in large software applications. CacheQL employs a static analysis tool to detect and map cache vulnerabilities to specific lines of code, and then uses dynamic analysis to identify the sensitive data that these vulnerabilities can target. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CacheQL by applying it to three significant projects: a cryptographic library, a web framework, and a machine learning library, revealing numerous cache vulnerabilities in each, including some in widely used components of the web framework. We also showcase how CacheQL can pinpoint the source of cache vulnerabilities to specific lines of code and discuss the characteristics of these vulnerabilities, which inform strategies for mitigating them. CacheQL is available under a permissive open-source license, and the accompanying case study is accessible online. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are notorious for their challenging training process, which often stalls due to difficulties in finding equilibrium between the generator and discriminator. This problem, known as mode collapse, has been a major obstacle in GAN development. Researchers have made numerous attempts to address the issue, but the reasons behind it remain unclear. This study investigates mode collapse by examining Hessian matrix properties in both generator and discriminator training. We analyze mode collapse by looking at Hessian eigenvalue spectra and assess the effectiveness of three common techniques: batch normalization, spectral normalization, and heuristic weight initialization. Our experiments, conducted on three datasets and three architectures, demonstrate that both batch normalization and spectral normalization can significantly improve mode collapse, but the underlying reasons differ: batch normalization enhances mode separation, while spectral normalization accelerates Hessian convergence. Furthermore, our study shows that the success of GAN training depends on the balance between mode collapse and convergence rates. We also provide theoretical support for our findings, providing a new understanding of GAN mode collapse. Overall, our study offers a new perspective on understanding GAN mode collapse and suggests that future research should focus on balancing mode collapse and convergence rates. The findings are expected to inspire innovative approaches to improving GAN mode collapse. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/taofdao/mixturegan. This paper investigates the existence of variational p-harmonic functions and their long-term behavior as they converge to either a p-harmonic function or a stationary p-harmonic system. Building upon previous research by Cherrier, Giacomoni and Sere, and Leonardi and Solonopolski, among others, the results demonstrate that a p-harmonic function with limited variations can evolve into a constant function through a process of gradient descent. This descent is driven by a nonlinear, nonlocal differential equation, which in the case of p equal to 2 reduces to a standard heat equation. A key aspect of this study is the identification of conditions under which a constant function can reach a state of equilibrium in a given environment. This is achieved by analyzing the behavior of p-harmonic functions in the vicinity of a constant function, which is modeled by a Dirichlet problem. A crucial component of this analysis is the identification of conditions for the weak sub/superopticity of the Dirichlet problem, which is established through a combination of variational methods and comparison principles. A significant outcome of this study is the derivation of a quantitative relationship between the rate of convergence of a p-harmonic function towards a constant function and the rate at which its gradient vanishes. This convergence is described in terms of both local and global norms, which in the case of p equal to 2 corresponds to the classical Harnack inequality. However, in the case of p greater than 2, this inequality is replaced by a more complex nonlinear relationship between the magnitude of certain quantities. We introduce a new cubic spline method for approximating one-dimensional functions, tailored to address issues arising from data noise and sharp function gradients. This approach is based on a monotone cubic spline model, offering an alternative to the popular Nadaraya-Watson estimator, with the additional benefit of ensuring positive function estimates. We demonstrate the improved performance of our method compared to existing non-monomial spline and kernel estimators for functions with specific singularities, such as the Cauchy distribution's density. This is supported by both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, highlighting the method's effectiveness in capturing function characteristics. In particular, the results show that our method can successfully recover the location and shape of a function's support when it follows a normal distribution. We also present a practical application of this approach in estimating the density of the Cauchy distribution from noisy data. Furthermore, the methods developed here can be adapted for estimating higher-dimensional monotone functions, with the potential for broader use in monotone regression tasks. The performance of our approach is evaluated through a Monte Carlo simulation, while a real-world application of the method is demonstrated using data collected from a scanning electron microscope. The process of removing haze from images has become increasingly popular due to advancements in deep learning technology. However, most existing methods evaluate dehazed images based on how well they preserve the details and colors of real-world scenes. While these metrics are useful, they can be limited by the availability of real-world data and the need to refer to a clear image for comparison. This paper introduces a new, data-independent metric called IDC (Intensity Dispersion of Color) to evaluate the quality of haze removal. IDC measures the variation in color intensity and takes into account both local and global aspects, using a combination of texture and structural features to capture the essence of haze removal. Experiments have shown that IDC outperforms existing methods in evaluating the quality of dehazed images, and it can be used to predict the quality of haze removal even when there are artifacts present. Furthermore, IDC has been integrated into a new, blind metric called Blind Dehazed Image Quality Assessment (BDIQA) to evaluate haze removal without any prior knowledge of the original image. BDQI, which uses a combination of convolutional neural networks and IDC, has been shown to be a reliable metric for assessing haze removal without any prior knowledge of the original image. Recent research has shown that deep learning models can be vulnerable to malicious attacks via their input data, specifically through adversarial samples designed by experts. These samples often require a thorough understanding of the model's architecture and training data, as well as manual manipulation of input features. This limitation restricts the effectiveness of such attacks, as inserting malicious input features can be a complex and computationally expensive process. To address this challenge, our proposed solution, DeepPayload, leverages a deep neural network to automatically generate adversarial samples by embedding malicious input features into DL models. This approach is particularly beneficial for black-box attacks, as it eliminates the need to know the model's architecture or training data, relying instead on input features and label information. Furthermore, our proposed solution employs a novel method for generating adversarial samples that is both robust and efficient, as demonstrated by experimental results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB datasets. The findings indicate that DeepPayload outperforms existing methods in terms of attack success rate, accuracy, and computational efficiency, especially when compared to other black-box attack methods. Notably, our proposed solution achieves a remarkable 100% attack success rate on the MNIST dataset, outperforming even the most advanced state-of-the-art attacks. This paper introduces Coded Assessment, a technique that utilizes a unique combination of a direct and a reflection signal to accurately determine the 3D position of a mobile device. Building on the concept of an "array code," Coded Assessment allows for the simultaneous transmission of data and a complex phase-shifted reflection signal. As a result, the receiver can use the reflected signal to obtain precise 3D position information, even in scenarios where the channel degrades the transmitted data. Furthermore, the technique enables the construction of a robust position estimation algorithm that can operate effectively in a wide range of environments. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of CAV, as it is capable of achieving a 3D positioning accuracy of up to several millimeters in a typical indoor setting. Moreover, the proposed technique offers a significant advantage over conventional methods, as it allows for a substantial increase in the number of possible array codes, thereby enabling a more accurate position information to be encoded. Finally, the technique has been demonstrated to be highly resilient against a variety of potential errors, including device and environmental inaccuracies, as well as a loss of signal strength. In particular, the proposed technique has been shown to be capable of operating effectively even in scenarios where the signal strength is reduced by a factor of 10. The experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of Coded Assessment for mobile device positioning in real-world settings. We present a new convergence indicator for Krylov methods, which can replace existing norms commonly used in research. This norm is based on the modification of the total residual and leverages second-order information, making it particularly suitable for Interior Point Methods in both linear and non-linear applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness through a comparison with CGRR and CGRRM in a linear Interior Point Method on a wide range of symmetric positive definite systems, outperforming the traditional CGRR and CGRRM indicators in terms of accuracy and speed. We also examine the robustness of our indicator in various Interior Point Method frameworks and note that it surpasses CGRRM in most cases. Additionally, we apply the proposed method to a non-linear setting, the augmented Lagrangian method, where it achieves comparable results to CGRRM. This work also explores the theoretical underpinnings of our indicator, drawing from existing research, and provides a framework for understanding its properties. We demonstrate that our indicator is a convex function and its minimum point represents the optimal solution to the problem at hand. This research lays the groundwork for the development of alternative indicators, expanding the scope of existing research in the field. In ensemble Q-learning, combining diverse value function estimates enhances control effectiveness by mitigating overconfidence issues. To address this limitation, a novel approach is proposed that leverages the representation diversity of expert estimates by incorporating the covariance matrix of action-state pairs into the linear combination. This modification is shown to significantly improve representation diversity, leading to superior performance in both value estimation and long-term control on various continuous control benchmarks. Notably, the proposed approach is compatible with most existing ensemble Q-learning methods and can be applied to other value estimation diversification techniques. Moreover, its benefits extend to other reinforcement learning settings, such as model-free policy evaluation and imitation learning. This versatile method provides a practical solution for improving representation and performance in a wide range of RL applications. By adjusting the leaves of the multileaf collimators, it's possible to project the beam onto various trajectories while maintaining a fixed collimator configuration, achieving an instantaneous beam shape control. Furthermore, this technique can be expanded to incorporate multiple multileaf collimators, effectively creating a multibeam system with controllable beamlets. We demonstrate the application of this technique to the Fermilab Intensity Frontier program and outline its potential for beam shaping in future projects. Additionally, this technique has far-reaching implications for the field of beam shaping and collimation, with potential applications extending beyond the proposed experiment. The development of 3D facial models is a crucial aspect in computer graphics and graphics design, and recent advancements have focused on creating realistic human-like faces. However, creating non-human faces is a significant challenge, and current methods often rely on user-defined parameters to control face features. These approaches typically fall into two categories: parameter-driven and data-driven. While parameter-driven methods offer flexibility in modifying face types, they often require users to manually define parameters, which can be a time-consuming and error-prone process. On the other hand, data-driven methods can automatically generate face types, but often struggle to create novel face features. To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, Cou3D, which combines the strengths of these two methods using a two-stage neural network architecture. Our model, TBGAN, first generates a face type from a user-defined face mesh, and then refines the face into a detailed mesh with a specified type. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through various experiments and showcase its potential applications in creating animated characters and designs. We introduce a groundbreaking, self-supervised image noise reduction method called Decay2Distill, which leverages image spatial disturbance as a surrogate task. This approach enables unsupervised image denoising by training on a single clean image and utilizing a noisy version as the disturbance signal. The method involves two stages: a decay process that refines the disturbance signal and uses it to guide denoising, followed by a regularization-based stage that refines both the disturbance signal and the denoised image. This enables the network to learn from the refined disturbance signal, which is then used to produce a clean image. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art supervised methods in image noise reduction, achieving an improvement of 0.36 dB in PSNR on the DIP2D dataset. Moreover, our method excels in robustness against various types of noise and can be applied to real-world images with complex noise patterns. Medical image classification systems that generalize across different patient groups are highly sought after but challenging to develop due to limited training data and domain disparities. A novel, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) approach is proposed to bridge the gap between source and target domains in medical image classification tasks. This framework utilizes feature disentanglement to isolate domain-invariant and unique information from target domain images. A graph convolutional network is employed to derive compact and discriminative feature representations from the disentangled images. Our experiments on various medical image datasets, including OCT scans of diabetic retinopathy and HRCT scans of lung diseases, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving competitive performance compared to supervised methods. Our results indicate that the proposed UDA framework outperforms existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 0.88, 0.82, and 0.83 in diabetic retinopathy grading, and an accuracy of 0.60, 0.56, and 0.61 in the detection and grading of emphysema and COPD, respectively. Real-time semantic segmentation is a key component of numerous computer vision applications.  Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved semantic segmentation performance, yet most existing models are not optimized for real-time processing.  To address this issue, a new model called the RTFormer is introduced, combining a lightweight backbone and a novel transformer architecture featuring a query sampling mechanism to enhance efficiency.  The lightweight backbone is optimized through a series of fine-tuning steps, while the query sampling mechanism is designed to strike a balance between speed and semantic segmentation quality. By leveraging the Q-value function, we can directly learn the essential states and policy. Our results show that this method can efficiently identify critical states and generate improved policies, even when working with limited data. Notably, it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational speed and effectiveness in solving complex tasks. Our work contributes to the growing body of research focused on state representation learning in RL. Our findings suggest that identifying essential states using Q-values is a promising direction for improving state representation learning and policy generation in RL. In this study, we examine the Bell associations on a finite warm unit disc that results from projecting a regular triangular lattice onto the unit disc. This extends a previous investigation by Cai et al. [Finet et al. 2022], which focused solely on a single temperature scenario. We demonstrate that at a certain temperature threshold, known as the M\"obius kink temperature, the Bell associations on the unit disc exhibit unique characteristics. Specifically, we show that above this temperature, the Bell associations on the unit disc are identical to those on the infinite disc. This finding is significant, as it implies that the large temperature limit of the Bell associations on the unit disc corresponds to the Bell associations on the infinite disc. We utilize a combination of analytical and computational approaches, including the examination of lattice coverings and simulations of random Bell associations, to support our results. Notably, our study reveals that the Bell associations on the small warm unit disc can be computed exactly, whereas those on the small warm hexagonal disc remains an open problem. This distinction highlights the complexity of the small warm hexagonal disc scenario, even in lattice covering terms. Finally, we present a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of the Bell associations on the small warm disc at various temperature settings. This theoretical framework is crucial in helping to further analyze the small warm disc scenario. The accompanying video resource is available at https://youtu.be/6qY8i2kxK8A. \bigskip

A novel approach to machine learning called Federated Learning allows multiple clients to collaborate on model training using local data. Despite its effectiveness, traditional FL methods often prioritize global data at the expense of client-specific information. In response, we've developed a customized training method that enables each client to adapt its trained model. By leveraging hypernetworks, we've successfully integrated this technique into various neural networks, including CNNs and LANs, and tested it on diverse datasets. The results demonstrate that our approach surpasses standard FL training on multiple fronts, including accuracy, client-specific performance, and overall efficiency. Additionally, we've demonstrated that hypernetworks equipped with FL can be effectively used to transfer knowledge and adapt to new tasks. The implications of this finding extend beyond machine learning to broader domains such as reinforcement learning and robotics. Overall, our research has shown that customized training with hypernetworks is a promising direction for improving the performance of neural networks in FL settings. Pretrained language models, specifically Multilingual BERT, are capable of processing multiple languages effectively. We investigate how this proficiency translates to cross-lingual information transfer, utilizing data from the Cross-lingual Text Classification task and language pairs including English and Russian, English and Spanish, and English and German. Our analysis reveals that BERT excels in a two-step process: first, it adapts English labels to other languages during training, and second, it leverages these labels to predict labels in target languages. We also find that fine-tuning Multilingual BERT on a target language significantly boosts its text classification accuracy compared to a standalone BERT model trained on English. This observation holds true across various languages, including those with distinct writing systems, and suggests that BERT's success in cross-lingual text classification stems from its ability to adapt English labels, rather than directly acquiring target language knowledge. We further observe that this adaptation process is primarily driven by the BERT model's self-supervised learning mechanism, particularly aligning the English and target language encodings of the tokenized labels. This insight offers valuable guidance for developing effective multilingual language models and transfer learning methods. Moreover, our findings have implications for understanding the mechanisms behind BERT's success in various NLP tasks. Finally, we propose a novel approach to data augmentation for multilingual text classification, specifically the "label translation" method, where a target language label is replaced with the English equivalent, and then back-translated into the target language. This technique is found to significantly enhance the text classification accuracy, achieving an improvement of up to 8.5%. In this study, we focus on a specific arrangement avoidance problem related to planar graphs, specifically undirected bipartite graphs, to explore the potential of using the corresponding complex structure for avoiding arrangements with a given ground set. Lastly, we propose several open problems and areas for further investigation in this field. The findings of this study are presented in a self-contained manner, making them accessible to a broader audience. Intelligent transportation systems heavily rely on accurate and timely traffic prediction, which is crucial for optimizing traffic flow. Current prediction models are often limited by their static nature, neglecting the dynamic evolution of traffic patterns. To address this issue, a new approach called Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Focus Network has been developed, which can effectively capture spatial-temporal correlations and dynamic changes in traffic flows. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the D-STFN in predicting traffic flows, particularly at an early stage of traffic incidents. Compared to existing methods, the D-STFN achieves significant improvements in mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE) on various datasets, showcasing its superior performance and efficiency in predicting traffic flows. This research introduces a novel speed and torque control strategy for electric motors, specifically aimed at mitigating parameter uncertainty when operating under unpredictable conditions. The proposed approach leverages a Gaussian Process-based probabilistic predictive model to estimate parameters in real-time, enabling anticipatory control. By integrating the GP-based model with an adaptive observer and a sliding window update mechanism, the controller can effectively handle parameter variations and system disturbances. Simulations conducted on a nonlinear DC motor model under uncertain conditions demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of anticipatory control on cooperative control design, specifically in scenarios involving parameter uncertainty. The results highlight the potential of anticipatory control to improve cooperative control performance. The proposed method is shown to outperform traditional adaptive control approaches, both with and without anticipatory mechanisms, in terms of convergence rate and transient performance. Finally, the research introduces a control strategy that utilizes the anticipatory mechanism to predict parameter changes and optimize cooperative control performance. The connection between the 1-Wasserstein distance and probability distributions' overlapping gaps has been underappreciated, despite its mathematical foundation. This note clarifies that the 1-Wasserstein distance essentially measures the magnitude of the difference between any pair of probability distributions. In the specific context of continuous distributions, it's actually equivalent to the length of the region between their overlapping portions. While this connection seems intuitive, the traditional definition of 1-Wasserstein distance has not been clearly linked to this physical interpretation in existing literature. This note aims to provide a clear and intuitive explanation for this relationship by providing a simple geometric proof. Furthermore, the blog post attached provides a more detailed and formal proof for readers interested in the mathematical aspects. A cutting-edge IoT offloading and computation model called Self-Managed IoT (SM-IoT) has been proposed, allowing users to manage their applications with complete control. This model comprises a cloud-based manager, a lightweight edge manager, and a user interface, giving users both edge computing benefits and centralized cloud computing, depending on their needs. The edge manager optimizes application performance by offloading tasks to the nearest edge node, while a user interface enables users to offload tasks between the edge and cloud, maximizing their control over application performance through task offloading decisions. A novel hierarchical matching algorithm has been developed to efficiently match tasks with suitable execution nodes, minimizing communication latency. The algorithm's effectiveness has been verified through experiments using real-world data from a large-scale 5G test network. The results demonstrate that SM-IoT can reduce task offloading latency by up to 28% and increase user satisfaction by up to 10.8% compared to existing approaches. The SM-IoT prototype has been successfully implemented and integrated into a 5G test network, showcasing its feasibility and effectiveness in real-world applications. Recent visual question answering (VQA) datasets, such as RAMEN, have made significant strides by incorporating multi-step open-ended questions and detailed answers. However, traditional VQA models have fallen short in handling the complexity of multi-step questions, leading to limited generalization outside of the training domain. This work addresses the model's inability to tackle multi-step VQA through a novel domain generalization approach, dubbed Enhanced RAMEN. By leveraging both global and local visual features, Enhanced RAMEN's cross-attention module effectively generates more accurate question representations. The model's cross-attention output is further refined by fusing local attention weights with cross-attention weights, resulting in a more reliable representation. Comprehensive evaluations on RAMEN and VQA-CP datasets confirm Enhanced RAMEN's ability to significantly improve cross-modal alignment and visual grounding, resulting in a 3.4% improvement in performance on RAMEN and a 2.1% improvement on VQA-CP. Actuaries utilize mortality models to analyze mortality rates and predict future mortality rates based on past data. This allows them to adjust insurance policies, determine premiums, and develop mortality forecasts. A recent study by Guo and others introduced a dynamic mortality model that incorporates factor models and autoregressive processes to account for time-varying mortality patterns. This research aims to determine whether factor loadings should be time-dependent or time-invariant within the dynamic model. We demonstrate that incorporating time-dependent factor loadings can be equivalent to including non-linear deterministic factors in the model, allowing us to leverage existing knowledge about non-linear deterministic factors to establish time-dependent factor loadings. We employ a stochastic process to represent the dynamic nature of factor loadings and show that it can be approximated by a specific type of process that captures periodic patterns. In cloud computing, particularly in virtual network embedding, the goal is to minimize the impact of failures on network availability. A new approach, referred to as Failure Aware Semi-decentralized VNE, is presented in this paper. This method involves the network operator having control over available network resources and the service provider having control over virtual resources. A key component of this algorithm is the ability to calculate the network reliability based on link failure scenarios and then use this information to optimize resource allocation for virtual networks. The algorithm was tested in cloud computing environments, specifically in fat-tree data center networks, using a proposed optimization function to measure algorithm efficiency. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of cost savings and network survival rates in the event of failures. Cost savings of up to 17.5% and 4.5% were observed compared to decentralized and semi-decentralized algorithms, respectively, while network survival rates were found to be 2.5% and 7% higher. The proposed algorithm demonstrates its ability to effectively manage network reliability in the event of failures on both small and large networks. Moreover, its computational efficiency makes it suitable for practical implementation in real-world network environments. A comparison with centralized algorithms showed that the proposed decentralized approach has a significantly lower average time complexity, making it a more viable option. Specifically, the proposed algorithm outperformed the centralized approach by an average of 98.5% in terms of computational efficiency. This research delves into the inherent characteristics of context-free grammar with the properties of context-free (context-sensitive) languages but allows for a more flexible class of choices for the production rules. Specifically, we examine the class of RLLS Grammars, which incorporates context-free (context-sensitive) grammars with rigid locally testable selection languages that exhibit finite ambiguity and possess a finite number of minimal equivalent grammars. By investigating RLLS Grammars, we aim to understand the distribution of their generated languages, their inherent ambiguity, and the potential benefits of using RLLS Grammars in comparison to traditional context-free grammars to create languages, mathematical structures, and sequences that are not replicable by their context-free counterparts. Furthermore, we present concrete examples of RLLS Grammars, their generated languages, and structural properties to demonstrate their potential and expand on existing research by extending the language model from LTL to RLLS, allowing for a broader class of languages, including those with unbounded repetition. By generalizing the language model, we demonstrate that RLLS Grammars can be more effective in generating a diverse range of structures, such as those found in formal languages, and present additional examples of their potential applications. Finally, we discuss the potential benefits of using RLLS Grammars in generating formal languages, their potential for a creative machine-based language production process, and the potential for a machine-based language production to be used by humans. Overall, our research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the creative potential of formal language generation.

A quantum system's dynamics is described by a density operator that evolves according to the Lindblad equation. Research has shown that the time derivative of Renyi entropy follows a specific formula. For the case of Renyi parameter alpha equal to one, it reduces to the von Neumann entropy. Studies have also found that the entropy change is linked to the rate of energy increase into the system. Moreover, the Lindblad spectrum has been identified as a measure of system energy-level distribution. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of both open and closed quantum systems using the Lindblad equation, specifically focusing on the case where energy is conserved. For the case of conserved energy, we demonstrate that the density operator remains unchanged. For the case of open systems, we find that the rate of energy increase into the system determines the direction of entropy flow. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entropy rate is related to the rate of energy increase into the surroundings. In the limit where the Renyi parameter approaches infinity, we find that the entropy rate becomes zero. Additionally, we show that the Lindblad spectrum remains unchanged despite changes in the system's initial conditions. For specific examples, we numerically calculate the Lindblad spectrum and compare it to the energy distribution in the system, finding a good match. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for understanding quantum entropy dynamics. For the complete article, see arXiv:2106.13126 [quant-ph]. As a result, the black hole's apparent horizon expands at a rate that depends on its charge $Q$, mass $M$, and Planck constant $\hbar$, at a rate of $O(q^2)$, $O(1)$, and $O(\hbar^2)$, respectively. Our findings indicate that the black hole's mass increases due to its charge, and we derive an expression for the energy emitted by the black hole in terms of its temperature and surface gravity. Our model further shows that the energy emitted follows the Hawking radiation law, and we calculate the energy emitted by a Schwarzschild black hole, finding it to be extremely small. Our research also extends to the gravitational field, finding that the event horizon's expansion rate depends on the same factors, at $O(q^2)$, $O(1)$, and $O(\hbar^2)$. To assess the feasibility of detecting exotic gauge bosons at lepton colliders' beam dump sites that employ energy recovery linacs, we examine the associated constraints and potential discoveries. Considering the High Intensity beam facility (HIBF) at J-PARC and the Super-FACET-II at DESY, we determine the bounds imposed by the non-observation of $e^+ e^-$ pair production, which translates to $U(1)_{L_1 L_2}$ gauge boson mass exceeding 10,000 GeV and a production cross section less than $10^{-7}$ fb. This analysis also reveals that similar sensitivity may be attained at the U-70 linac of the Budker Institute, while a potential discovery could be made with a smaller beam current, resulting in a mass lower bound of 2,000 GeV and a production cross section lower bound of $10^{-5}$ fb. Furthermore, we outline the requisite detectors and prospective discoveries that could arise from conducting these beam dump experiments. Additionally, we discuss the potential for utilizing these experiments to establish the existence of a $U(1)_{L_1 L_2} \otimes U(1)_{L_3 L_4}$ gauge symmetry by measuring the $e^+ e^- \mu^+ e^-$ production rate. In the field of particle physics, reconstructing the paths of particles in real-time is a critical challenge, particularly for the next generation of High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider detectors. To address this, our research presents a novel approach utilizing Graph Neural Networks on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays, capable of performing the instantaneous reconstruction task in a single time step. This method leverages Graph Neural Networks to enhance particle track reconstruction accuracy and robustness across a wide range of detector conditions, outperforming conventional methods by a margin of 20-30% and achieving a 20% improvement in track reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, our implementation of this innovative model on Field-Programmable Gate Array technology yields exceptional performance, with a 3.5 ns latency and a 1.07 MHz processing rate at a 30 MiB/s input bandwidth, paving the way for real-time processing applications in various fields. This method is particularly suited for the next generation of advanced particle detectors, where precise track reconstruction is critical for efficient data analysis. With its compact design and efficient processing capabilities, this approach has significant implications for the development of novel track reconstruction algorithms and data processing systems, particularly for the next generation of High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider detectors. Handling continuous variables in classification problems can be efficiently managed through discretization, a process that simplifies the variables into discrete values. Existing discretization methods, however, are often limited in their ability to effectively handle the variables due to their reliance on a single optimization strategy. In this research, a novel criterion for discretization is proposed by combining two essential properties - a maximum relevance property and a minimum variation property - to improve the performance of the na\"ive Bayes classifier. Through experiments on various datasets, the proposed discretization approach, named Max-relevance-min-variation discretization, demonstrated its ability to outperform other methods in terms of overall accuracy, specifically for the na\"ive Bayes classifier. Additionally, the proposed criterion can be easily integrated with other classification algorithms. Its efficacy was validated through further experiments on a large-scale dataset, the ImageClef 2011 dataset, using a k-nearest neighbor classifier. The proposed method achieved a higher accuracy rate compared to traditional discretization methods, a finding that is consistent with prior research. This research investigates the effect of using pre-trained speech characteristics in automatic gender recognition for overlapped dialogue. Unlike previous studies that have mostly used isolated utterances, our experiment involves using speaker-independent features extracted from pre-trained WavLM encoders for speech recognition. We conducted an experiment using three different approaches to extract features and found that the best approach was using the WavLM encoder's intermediate output for a 3-second speech window. We achieved a high accuracy of 97.7% in evaluating the results using a large dataset of overlapped conversations. We also observed that the WavLM encoder's performance improved with the presence of at least two speakers in the dataset. A thorough analysis revealed that the WavLM encoder's intermediate output effectively captured speaker characteristics, making it a suitable choice for automatic gender recognition in overlapped conversations. To our knowledge, this research is the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of using pre-trained speech characteristics for gender recognition in overlapped dialogue. The findings of this research can contribute to improving the development of robust and practical speech recognition systems that can handle real-world conversations. The source code and data for this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/taofdoan/gender_recognition_in_overlapped_dialogue. Reinforcement Learning algorithms have excelled in solving complex problems by discovering optimal policies in intricate environments, but they struggle when faced with dynamic environments that evolve over time. To address this limitation, we have developed an innovative approach that leverages historical data to update an existing RL policy as the environment changes. Our method, Temporal Change Reinforcement Learning, uses a temporal change detector to identify shifts in the environment and then applies a policy updater to adjust the policy in response. Through experimentation, we have found that this approach can achieve near-optimal results in a wide range of dynamic environments. Moreover, we have demonstrated that this method can be efficiently applied even in environments with vast state and action spaces. Finally, we have shown that this technique can be applied to a variety of real-world problems, including the control of a quadcopter robot and the optimization of online advertising display strategies. The task of technical name standardization enables machines to link different forms of technical terminology. In contrast, the goal of technical term traceability involves identifying the original, standardized terms originally used in a technical text. Current methods for generating technical terms typically rely on language models that are trained on standardized data, leading to reduced connection precision due to biased predictions. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to improve the language generator's ability to produce more accurate connections between technical terms by leveraging pre-existing models. We achieve this by utilizing a pre-trained BERT-as-a-encoder model to generate context-aware representations of technical terms, and then employing a BERT-as-a-generator model to produce candidate connections. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this technique significantly enhances the language generator's performance and produces more accurate connections between technical terms. Furthermore, the approach is proven effective in both English and Chinese languages. The proposed method is also shown to be more resilient to class imbalance issues that commonly affect the technology term traceability task. The 'jsonme' command is designed to assess the compliance of a JSON file against a set of sample instances, utilizing a concept similar to software testing where test cases are used to verify the functionality of a program. This tool allows developers to evaluate the generalizability of a JSON schema by comparing its instance set against a larger pool of sample instances, thus providing an objective measure of how well the schema is representative of the entire domain. The command offers three primary evaluation metrics - equivalence, coverage, and accuracy - each calculated based on a set of sample instances, with accuracy specifically dependent on the presence of diverse instances. In addition to its evaluation capabilities, 'jsonme' also includes a mode for validating the conformity of a JSON file against a set of sample instances, ensuring that it aligns with all test cases. This framework can be applied to the study of other phenomena within thermal environments, such as birefringence and dielectric properties. In the presence of a charge density ripple, the transverse displacement and electric potential distributions within a semiconductor conform to specific patterns. When the charge density ripple is static, these patterns remain unchanged over time. However, when the charge density ripple evolves over time, the transverse displacement and electric potential exhibit periodic temporal behavior. By applying conformal mapping, these patterns can be linked to well-known mathematical functions, namely the elliptic, hyperbolic, and trigonometric types. A key characteristic of these patterns is that they are invariant under time reversal when the charge density ripple is stationary. Our analysis reveals that using a batch size equal to the number of model parameters is optimal in the sense of achieving the minimum oracle complexity. However, this is an idealized scenario, as in practical applications, we need to consider various parameters, including learning rates and regularization strengths, which are additional sources of stochasticity. Our theoretical results show that using a batch size equal to the number of parameters is still optimal when these extrinsic sources of noise are present, while indicating that a batch size or its square root can be used as a control parameter to minimize oracle complexity in the context of deep learning. Our findings are supported by experimental evidence. Ultimately, we propose a novel approach to learning hyperparameters, which is essential for deep learning, by using a critical batch size as a control parameter. Our numerical experiments also demonstrate the benefits of this approach in practice. The camera's 16 modules each house 96 pixels, bringing the total to 4608 polarization-sensitive pixels, which aim to measure the cosmic microwave background's polarization signals at three frequencies: 270 GHz, 450 GHz, and 500 GHz. A custom mirror assembly consisting of 32, 64, and 72 elements is used for each frequency, which includes additional auxiliary elements that enable light to reach specific pixels. The purpose of these auxiliary elements is to stabilize the optical response, reduce system noise, and facilitate the calibration process. The design of the auxiliary elements, including their functionality, has been documented in this paper along with simulation results and on-sky data from SPT-3G's first observing season. The data confirms that the auxiliary elements successfully stabilized the camera's response, even in the presence of long-term temperature fluctuations. The implementation of the auxiliary elements is also credited for achieving an overall optical efficiency of 65% for the SPT-3G camera, exceeding initial projections. The primary objective of image separation is to isolate distinct objects within a composite image, where each object is represented by a latent representation. Traditional approaches to image separation involve training a single model that simultaneously optimizes the object latent representations and the separator's overall performance. This approach, however, is plagued by the issue of shared optimization gradients between representation isolation and separator performance, hindering the separator's ability to accurately separate objects. In this research, we introduce a novel semi-supervised approach to image separation that decouples the optimization of object latent representations from the separator's performance, thereby enabling the generation of realistic images. Our semi-supervised model consists of a generative network and a conditional adversarial network that work in tandem to optimize the generation of high-quality training images, thereby facilitating effective isolation of the object latent representations. Our approach, which leverages the StyleGAN framework, is shown to outperform current state-of-the-art image separation techniques in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. This study introduces a new system to assess the mobility of a rover in soft terrain during its approach and landing phase.

We introduce an innovative IV estimator that leverages a unique combination of partial least squares methods, known as profound partial least squares. This new approach seamlessly integrates both low-dimensional and high-dimensional data analysis techniques, allowing it to effectively handle complex, non-linear relationships in IV models. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we demonstrate that our estimator outperforms existing alternatives, and it also offers computational efficiency and state-of-the-art properties even with large datasets. Furthermore, our method's flexibility is demonstrated across a range of practical applications, including the analysis of various types of financial assets and its potential for use in sentiment analysis. The estimator's code has been made publicly accessible via the repository found at https://github.com/soderbergtheprofound/ppl. Supplying additional results in appendix D, we also replicate a well-known empirical study to validate the estimator's performance. Lastly, a comprehensive review of IV overidentification tests highlights the scarcity of available tools for evaluating the IV model's overidentification in the specific context of profound PLS. Consequently, further research is suggested to address this knowledge gap. This paper introduces a novel approach to monocular 3D object recognition, leveraging a depth estimation network to dynamically adjust the information flow in a 3D object detector. The method involves two interconnected networks: a depth estimation network conditioning information flow for depth prediction, and a 3D object detection network generating depth-related features to refine depth predictions. These networks exchange information via a novel dynamic routing mechanism, aggregating depth predictions with features from multi-scale cost volumes to produce refined depth estimates. Notably, the information flow between the networks is contingent upon the depth prediction, allowing for a dynamic exchange of information. The proposed method is validated through experiments on KITTI, nuScenes, and SUNCG datasets, yielding a substantial 2.5-4.2 mAP improvement over existing state-of-the-art approaches in the open-world KITTI 3D detection benchmark. Moreover, the method demonstrates impressive performance in the more challenging indoor environment of SUNCG, outperforming existing solutions by 6.0 mAP. Code and models are available for public access at https://github.com/autolab-qtec/depth-conditioned-dynamic-IT. This implies that higher fractional orders lead to more stringent stability conditions in the sense of Ulam--Hyers. Consequently, our results provide valuable insights into the properties of nonlinear $\Psi$-Hilfer fractional differential equations and their stability characteristics. Ultimately, our work contributes to the existing literature by offering a comprehensive understanding of these equations' global presence and Ulam--Hyers stability. Our method has been applied to a ring resonator and a microcavity and has been validated through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we have studied the excitation dynamics of polariton condensates within the exciton-laser framework, and our findings show that the exciton loss plays a crucial role in this process. The results also reveal that the exciton loss leads to a decrease in the condensate's lifetime and an increase in its effective temperature. The influence of exciton loss on the excitation dynamics of polariton condensates is consistent with previous experimental observations. Attribribution-based explanations are gaining importance in the field of complex decision-making systems.  However, existing research primarily focuses on the quality of these explanations and their transparency, whereas their reliability remains poorly understood.  In this paper, we introduce a new concept of stability to assess these explanations and provide a set of guidelines for measuring their reliability in various scenarios.  Furthermore, we develop a framework for quantifying the impact of attribute importance on system stability and conduct a comprehensive simulation study to validate our approach.  The study reveals both beneficial and negative effects of attribute importance on system stability, and highlights the potential for attributability-based explanations to improve the trustworthiness of complex decision-making systems.  Our findings also serve as a foundation for future research to investigate novel methods for generating stable and reliable explanations in various application domains.

A key concept in understanding thermal equilibrium states of Rayleigh-Bénard convection is the marginally-stable state, where fluctuations around a steady roll solution remain bounded as time progresses. Building on the prior work of Owerin and Tkachenko, we employ a different approach to investigate this concept, starting with a different representation of the marginal stability equation. This representation highlights the critical role of the spectral weight, a measure of the importance of fluctuations in the energy balance. Our findings reveal that there are infinitely many marginally-stable states, each characterized by a unique spectral weight, and we develop a systematic method for classifying and analyzing them. Notably, we identify a subset of marginally-stable states that emerge from the primary thermal convection equilibrium via a distinct detuning process. Our theoretical framework provides a robust foundation for understanding the behavior of marginally-stable states in thermal equilibrium, and we plan to apply this work to study thermal turbulence. The underlying principles developed here will also have broader implications for understanding marginally-stable states in other complex systems. A novel approach for estimating rock permeability from 3D micro-CT images is proposed, utilizing a physics-informed convolutional neural network. This model is based on the Navier-Stokes equation and incorporates only the relative permeability tensor, resulting in a more efficient and interpretable estimation. Utilizing direct numerical simulation data, the proposed network was trained and demonstrated to effectively predict various permeability tensors, even at reduced resolution. This success highlights the potential of the developed method for estimating rock properties in subsurface geoscience applications. Neural Networks that incorporate physical knowledge, often referred to as physics-informed neural networks, have successfully applied physics theories to various complex systems. In particular, their ability to quickly learn ordinary differential equations has garnered significant attention. However, assessing their accuracy remains a challenge due to the inherent tradeoff between neural network complexity and computational overhead. In this study, we developed a novel metric to evaluate the efficiency of these networks by combining multiple existing metrics. We tested our approach on a set of classic ODEs and found that the proposed method effectively assesses neural network performance across different complexity levels. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the increased computational resources required by these networks yield more accurate predictions for complex systems. In contrast, simpler models may be sufficient for precise predictions within a specific timeframe but fail to accurately replicate long-term dynamics, highlighting the need for a comprehensive evaluation method for PI-NNs. Our work aims to bridge the gap between neural network complexity and accuracy, paving the way for the development of more effective models for complex systems. This research introduces Gemino, a groundbreaking video compression system combining the capabilities of neural compression and error correction to efficiently and robustly transmit videos over networks. Gemino's innovative pipeline integrates a real-time neural video compressor with a sophisticated error correction algorithm, capable of accurately restoring complex video elements, such as text and shapes, which current systems often fail to achieve. Through a thorough evaluation of Gemino's performance under various network conditions, we demonstrate its ability to achieve exceptional compression efficiency and maintain exceptional visual quality. Gemino significantly reduces the transmission size by approximately 6.5 times and maintains a high video quality metric (PSNR) of 24.9 dB on average, while its performance remains remarkably stable across various network scenarios. Moreover, Gemino's error correction algorithm, utilizing a mere 0.1% of the transmission bandwidth, achieves remarkable fidelity in restoring complex video elements and maintains a high video quality metric (PSNR) of 19.5 dB on average. The innovative design of Gemino enables it to adapt seamlessly to various network conditions, resulting in exceptional compression efficiency and robust text and shape recovery. Capturing three-dimensional information of dynamic scenes using light field cameras has become a significant area of interest. The process of obtaining depth from light field data is complex, involving the interaction of multiple factors such as viewpoint, aperture, and occlusion. Existing methods for depth estimation in these scenes typically rely on a single, linear model that fails to account for the intricacies of real-world settings. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to depth estimation that takes into consideration the factors affecting depth accuracy, specifically occlusion. The proposed model is composed of two components: the first estimates the impact of occlusion on depth accuracy and the second generates the depth map itself. The impact of occlusion is assessed by comparing the depth map with a reference image, resulting in a continuous value between 0 and 1. The reference image is obtained by applying a spatial transformation to the input image, which is then passed through a convolutional neural network. The network, named Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (Orec), is trained to generate a depth map that is consistent with the input image and a reference image, while also accounting for the impact of occlusion. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated using a publicly available dataset, demonstrating its ability to generate accurate depth maps in real-world settings.
